question: Coral reefs are ‘tropical forests’ that host 25 % of marine life, protect coastlines and support the global food chain. Although we have the most advanced tools for mapping and monitoring marine ecosystems, such as the Copernicus Marine Service (CMEMS), the MAES initiative and the European Digital Twin Ocean, the Commission stated in 2021 (Ref. E-001607/2021) that mapping of European reefs is incomplete.
At the same time, coral reefs continue to deteriorate, while the implementation of the Nature Restoration Law is still ongoing.

Given that, in accordance with Article 56 of UNCLOS, Member States exercise sovereign rights within their EEZs for the protection and management of marine resources and that the EU has exclusive competence for their conservation, issues are cropping up in relation to coordination, operational implementation and the use of available tools. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following: 1.
What specific measures has it taken since 2021 to fully map reefs within Member States’ maritime zones, including their EEZs?
How is it ensured that Member States make use of available Union tools to actively exercise their sovereign rights to protect marine ecosystems?

Does it intend to propose binding measures to strengthen the practical implementation of Member States’ rights and obligations in their EEZs, in particular as regards the protection and restoration of reefs?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (17.7.2026) Member States are required under the Marine Strategy Framework1 and Habitats Directives2 to monitor and protect habitats, including reefs, in the marine waters where they have jurisdiction. The Nature Restoration Regulation3 further introduces binding mapping and restoration targets for marine habitats.

Member States’ plans for mapping and restoration of habitats will be shared in their draft national restoration plans by 1 September 2026. As regards fisheries measures, while the EU has exclusive competence to adopt acts on the conservation of marine biological resources under the common fisheries policy4, Member States are responsible for their implementation.
To support Member States, the Commission is promoting the use of monitoring, data and modelling tools through technical support and EU funding programmes5.

The Copernicus Marine Service6 provides observations of parameters such as sea-surface temperature, ocean currents and acidification; EMODnet7 provides access to marine in-situ data on parameters, including the distribution of coralligenous structures; the future Digital Twin of the Ocean8 will have the capacity to simulate reef ecosystems to inform conservation strategies.

The new OceanEye initiative9 provides a strategic framework to reinforce these efforts by strengthening ocean observation capacities, improving access to marine data and intelligence, and fostering cooperation between Member States, research organisations and international partners.
The Commission is currently preparing a proposal to revise the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, with the aim to progress towards good environmental status of EU seas10.
